role: Vice President, Design Engineering, Duke Power Company
stance_basis: submits detailed technical corrections and amendments to the Draft EIS on behalf of Duke Power Company while supporting the project's license application
summary: W. H. Owen, Vice President of Design Engineering at Duke Power Company, submitted a formal letter on January 5, 1976 enclosing Amendment 1 to the license application and Duke's comments on the Draft Environmental Impact Statement. His submission included numerous technical corrections and clarifications to the DEIS, covering design specifications, environmental data, and factual errors, indicating support for the project contingent on accurate representation of Duke's plans. He also provided a sworn affidavit attesting to the accuracy of the submitted materials.
complaint_summary: Duke Power Company, through W. H. Owen's submission, provides extensive technical corrections and clarifications to the Draft EIS covering design dimensions, land use data, flora and fauna descriptions, socio-economic figures, and water quality information, requesting revisions to numerous sections of the DEIS.

statement.text:
SUMMARY SHEET
Page 1 - Paragraph 3
Item number 2 would be in better perspective if it were re-worded to read: "elimination of approximately 2.3 miles (1.3 surface acres) of trout stream representing about 1.0 percent of the state's trout stream mileage, and 0.23 percent of its surface area (this does not include Lake Jocassee, a 7,565 acre reservoir constructed by Buke Power Company, which supports a trout fishery)".
The paragraph has been revised. Staff concludes that the sentence is adequate with this minor revision.

1. DESCRIPTION OF PROPOSED ACTION
1.3 Land Requirements
Page 1-8
Paragraph two should be re-worded to read: "Upon completion of the project, the 40-acre spoil area - constfuction yard will be reforested except for an area for a future 525 KV switchyard that is planned. The future switchyard area will be stabilized, planted, and maintained with grass or other ground cover until needed for switchyard use.
Section 1.3 has been revised.
1.4.1 Project Works and Reservoirs
Page 1-9
The last paragraph states that the underground powerhouse would be 65 feet wide and concrete lined. The chamber will not be concrete lined and will be 75 feet wide.
Section 1.4.1 has been revised.
Exhibit W Figures 1.4-1, 1.4-2, 1.4-3, 1.4-4 and Exhibit V Sheet 2 have been revised by Amendment 1. DEIS Figures 1-3, 1-5, 1-6, 1-7 and 1-4 should be revised accordingly.
Figures have been revised.
The lest paragraph states that two units will be equipped with starting motors. This should be changed to four motors, one for each unit, per Exhibit M - page 2, Amendment 1.
Section 1.4.1 has been revised.
Page 1-13
The first paragraph states that a 30 ton bridge crane would handle the draft tube tunnel gates. The draft tube tunnel gates may be eliminated by descring the surge chambers.
Section 1.4.1 has been revised.
Paragraph two makes reference to a surge chamber. Surge chambers may not be needed. Preliminary hydraulic transient analysis indicates that the surge chambers can be deleted by using two tailrace tunnels leading out to Lake Jocassee, one for the first two units, and the second for Units 3 and 4. See Exhibit W, Figure 1.4-2, Amendment 1.
Section 1.4.1 has been revised.
Paragraph four states that the upper 6 foot of Lake Jocassee is reserved for the use of future pumped storage projects. The lower 6 foot of Lake Jocassee (elevation 1080 - 1086) are reserved for future pumped storage projects.
Section 1.4.1 has been revised.

1,4.2 Tai luster Features
Page 1-14
Peragraph five says that a velocity of 7.0 feet per second is in the discharge channel after passing through the trash rack structure. This is incorrect and should read that 6.8 feet per second velocity occurs in the discharge structure openings, not after passing through the trash rack structure. See Exhibit W. Section 1.4.3, Amendment 1.
Section 1.4.2 has been revised.
Page 1-16
Paragraph one states that a 5.8 feet per second velocity occurs in the Intake channel before the water enters the trashrack structure. During pumping, a 5.6 feet ar second velocity is in the structure openings, not in the channel before entering the trashracks. See Exhibit W, Section 1.4.3, Amendment 1.
Section 1.4.2 has been revised.
1.4.3 Access Roads and Tunnels
Page 1-16
The access tunnel to the surge chamber galley may not be required. Based on preliminary hydraulic transient analysis, the surge chamber can be eliminated.
Section 1.4.3 has been revised.
1.4.4 Transmission Facilities
Page 1-17
Paragraph three gives the transmission tower dimensions as 120 feet high and 40 feet square at the tower base. This has been revised by Améndment 1 (Exhibit W, Section 1.4.4) to a height varying from 96 feet to 176 feet and a base from 28 feet to 68 feet square at the ground line.
Section 1.4.4 has been revised.
1.6 Operational and Maintenance Procedures
Page 1-25
The last sentence in paragraph two states that in the event of flooding, egress could be negotiated by two access tunnels and the vertical bus shaft. This should be changed to one access tunnel and the vertical bus shaft.
Section 1.6 has been revised.

2. DESCRIPTION OF THE EXISTING ENVIRONMENT
2.1.1 Land Uses
Page 2-1
Data from Crescent Land and Timber Corporation show that no longleaf pine (P. australis), slash pine (P. elliotti), and loblolly (P. taeda) has been hervested. However, tulip poplar (Liriodendron tulipifera), pitch pine (P. rigida), and Virginia pine (P. virginiana) are frequently harvested and should be added to the list.
Section 2.1.1 has been revised.
2.1.1.1 Recreation
Page 2-3
Highway 107 is located two miles west of the project, not three miles as stated in paragraph three of DEIS.
Section 2.1.1.1 has been revised.
Page 2-4
Paragraph four, the public access areas being developed initially around the reservoir should be four, not five as stated in the DES. See Exhibit R, sheet 1.
Section 2.1.1.1 has been revised.
2.1.2 Topography, Physiography, and Geology
Page 2-5
The last sentence in paragraph tro should be reworded to read: "They are folded, faulted, crushed, and sheared, all of which has accelerated their weathering and decomposition to maximum depths in excess of 100 feet in certain areas", per Exhibit V, Appendix 1, Table 1.
See revised Section 2.1.2.
Paragraph four states that natural materials available for construction appear marginal and will require careful design and proper construction control. Investigations have shown that adequate materials are available, per the License Application, Section 5, Pages 6 and 7 and Exhibit V, Appendix 1, Table 3.
Staff feels this sentence is accurate as stated and requires no revision.
Paragraph five mentions concern regarding seepage losses through the foundation rock. A grout curtain will be placed in the creek bottom and blanketing with soil will be used where soil cover over weathered rock is relatively thin. See Exhibit W, Appendix i.
Section 2.1.2 has been revised.
2.1.3 Solls
Page 2-6
The first sentence in paragraph four should be reworded to read: "These soils are subject to rapid erosion when exposed".
Section 2.1.3 has been revised.
2.2.1 Flora
BK-DES
2-1

Page 2-6, 2-7
The work of Dr. C. Leland Rodgers and Joseph E. Green, Jr., contained in Exhibit W, Appendix D, presents a thorough list of plant communities and species occurring in the project area. Also, the pamphlet prepared by Dr. Rodgers, entitled "Flowers, Ferns, Shrubs, and Trees found at Keowee-Toxaway" (Copy enclosure #1) is a substantially complete list for the mountains and foothills of Oconee, Pickens, Greenville and Spartanburg Counties, South Carolina, as well as for the adjacent North Carolina countles of Jackson, Transylvania, Henderson, and Polk.
See revised Section 2.2.1.
2.2.2.1 Viidlife
Page 2-14
The last paragraph states that the Pileated woodpecker is uncommon. Personnel of Crescent Land and Timber Corporation report that the Pileated Woodpecker is common in the Jocassee area. Crescent's timber management and harvesting plans have provisions for preservation of den trees for both cavity dwelling birds and mammals.
Section 2.2.2 has been revised.
Page 2-15
First paragraph, the name clemsonee should be dropped because subspecies are Section 2.2.2 has been revised. no longer recognized in Plethodon Jordani. (Exhibit W, Subsection 2.2.3.1, Amendment 1)
2.2.2.2 Aquatic Fauna
Page 2-25
Table 2-5 would be in better perspective by adding a column for the trout entitled "average weight per individual" with values for the three samples areas of 1.2 oz., 2.5 oz., and 0.9 oz., respectively.
Staff feels that this table is adequate as presented.
2.2.3.1 Flora
Page 2-28
Twenty-six specimens of Fothergilla major were transplanted out of the project area to suitable nearby habitats during summer 1974. In May 1975, these individuals were checked and found to be thriving. See Ex. W, Subsection 2.2.3.1, Amendment 1.
Section 2.1.3.1 has been revised.
Page 2-30
Only five of the 25 rare or uncommon plants listed here occur in the general area of the project. Those species are pink lady-slipper, umbrella-leaf, Oconee bells, and loosestrife. Loosestrife is the only rare species occurr- See also Section 4.2.1. ing in the immediate project area. Twenty-two loosestrife specimens were transplanted out of the project area.to suitable nearby habitats in summer 1974, see Exhibit W, Subsection 2.2.3.1, Amendment 1. The only other rare
Section 2.7.3.1 has been revised.

species in the area is Oconee bells, which occurs in some places along the proposed transmission line route. Dr. C. Leland Rodgers (Exhibit W, Appendix 6) has stated that Duke's plans for constructing transmission lines should result in these Oconee bells not being disturbed.
Staff concurs provided that Dr. Rodger's stated conditions are met.
2.2.3.2 Fauna
Page 2-32
Paragraph three, the Clemson salamander, and the other races of Plethodon Jordani, are no longer recognized as subspecies. Their status has been reduced to that of different color phases. These color phases do not occur In local areas as originally thought, rather, they are each widely scattered throughout the range of P. jordani. Thus, the Clemson phase is not restricted to the Bad Creek area. (See Conant, R. 1975. A field guide to reptiles and amphibians of eastern and central North America. 2nd edition. Houghton Mifflin Co. Boston. Also see other data previously supplied in Enclosure #21 of supplemental information of 8 Oct. 1974).
Section 2.2.3.2 has been revised.
2.3 Socio-Economic Considerations
Page 2-33
1970 combined population of Ocnee and Pickens Counties is 99,684 from Census of Population, not 99, 324 as stated in the first paragraph.
Section 2.3 has been corrected.
Page 2-36
Combined Pickens and Oconee County construction employment - 11.07 percent of the total number of workers in the two counties as shown in Table 2-8. Duke's Table 2-8 has been corrected. calculations of Table 2-8 conclude that it should be changed to 10.07.
2.4.3.3 Water Quality
Page 2-52
Figure 2-14, "Horsefeather River" should read "Horsepasture River."
Figure 2-14 has been corrected.
Page 2-61
Figure 2-17, in the plot for 1/21/74, the oxygen and temperature labels should be reversed.
Figure 2-17 has been corrected.

. ENVIRONMENTAL IMPACTS OF THE PROPOSED ACTION
3.1.1 Land Peatures and Uses
Page 3-1
According to Crescent Land and Timber, loblolly is not a species of commercial value in this area. The three acres occupied by the transmission towers will also be seeded and not excluded as indicated. The 31-mile long corridor will extend from the vicinity of the Lower Whitewater Falls to Table Bock State Park.
Section 3.1.1 has been revised.
3.1.1.2 Scenic and Esthetic Resources
Page 3-3
The second paragraph should be reworded to read: "During construction activity, landscape characteristics of the area within the upper reservoir site would change drastically, with some changes in the surrounding areas. This impact would be temporary for the duration of those activities."
Section 3.1.1 has been revised to clarify this paragraph.
Add to paragraph three: "Most of this acreage would be in the reservoir basin and would be ultimately inundated."
Section 3.1.1 has been revised to include this point.
3.1.2.1 Flora
Page 3-4
In paragraph two dealing with the clearing for the transmission line, applicant intends to clear around tower locations and in areas where a line clearance of 30 feet above the tree tops is not possible. As proposed, clearing of the transmission line would be accomplished by selective cutting as transmission towers would be placed on the highest elevations when possible. Selective cutting will be used to the fullest extent possible minimizing the need to clear all vegetation from beneath the lines.
Section 3.1.2 has been revised.
3.1.2.2 Fauna
Page 3-6
in the third paragraph, the DEIS states that the Staff are uncertain as to the exact impact of the construction upon populations of endangered species. Endangered species is assumed to mean those on the published list of endangered species. There is no evidence that any of these species inhabit the project area with the exception of a lone sighting of a bald eagle in flight at Lake Keowee on August 18, 1974.
